proposed_edges.relationship: In the interview “Acts of Literature II” (2018), Greenblatt credits Walter Benjamin, alongside other thinkers, with helping New Historicism escape the base/superstructure dichotomy.
proposed_edges.map_label: Benjamin as a resource for New Historicism
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the journal PDF, p. 124, Greenblatt’s first answer, beginning “For better or worse”: after identifying Foucault as helpful in escaping the base/superstructure dichotomy, he adds “but so too” and names Benjamin, de Certeau, Marin and Geertz. This is Greenblatt’s retrospective acknowledgment in an e-mail interview conducted in March 2018 and published in 2018, not a dated claim about a specific Benjamin work or evidence of personal contact. No Benjamin book was read for this proposal. Distinct from the existing Foucault and Geertz edges; both endpoints exist and there is no existing Benjamin–Greenblatt edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the interview “Acts of Literature II” (2018), Greenblatt credits Michel de Certeau, alongside other thinkers, with helping New Historicism escape the base/superstructure dichotomy.
proposed_edges.map_label: De Certeau as a resource for New Historicism
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the journal PDF, p. 124, first answer: the same sentence that credits Foucault extends the acknowledgment with “but so too” to a list explicitly including Michel de Certeau. Claim limited to this retrospective acknowledgment of an intellectual resource, with no particular de Certeau work, exclusive allegiance or personal relationship inferred. Interview conducted March 2018; original publication 2018. De Certeau’s books and Greenblatt’s foreword to The Possession at Loudun were not read here. No existing de Certeau–Greenblatt edge was found in the supplied entry or the full graph.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Acts of Literature II” (2018), Greenblatt identifies frustration with the Marxist literary criticism of Althusser and Lukács, to which he had initially turned against American formalism, as one impetus for New Historicism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the journal PDF, p. 124, first answer: Greenblatt describes his “frustration” with Marxist literary criticism, explicitly naming Lukács and Althusser, before explaining his wish to bring the whole cultural field into play and escape the base/superstructure dichotomy. This supports a bounded retrospective dissatisfaction with Althusser’s literary-critical approach; it does not support a detailed refutation of an Althusser text, rejection of all Marxism, or a claim that Williams ceased to matter. No Althusser original was read. Original interview publication 2018; the date does not purport to date the earlier change of mind. Althusser is an existing endpoint; Lukács is not.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Loitering in the Piazza” (1988), Greenblatt praises Giovanni Levi’s archival persistence in Inheriting Power but argues that insufficient engagement with the exorcist’s inner life weakens its speculation about his belief in his healing powers.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary review read on the journal’s own site. Exact HTML locators: paragraph beginning “I confess that for me” praises Levi’s “dogged patience”; penultimate paragraph, beginning “Did he think to recoup”, questions how well the account supports Levi’s conjecture about the exorcist’s belief; final paragraph calls the project “modest and quietly courageous”. The criticism concerns this explanatory limit, not wholesale rejection of microhistory. Issue date is 27 October 1988, vol. 10, no. 19; review pp. 18–19, but HTML paragraph locators, not a page image, were checked. Levi’s book itself remains unread; its 1988 English publication is not substituted for the date of the Italian original.

No original Davis passage acknowledging the supposed borrowing was verified here. These possible debts or exchanges remain held for unread primary evidence; praise alone is not converted into influence.
